clues.text: (Hi, I'm Fred McGergle at WFLD in Chicago)   This French post-impressionist who only lived to be 31 could be considered to be the world's first dot-matrix printer - his masterpiece "A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte," in front of which I am currently standing, was acquired by the Art Institute of Chicago in 1923 as a gift from trustee Frederic Bartlett

(Hi, I'm Ken Jennings, and I superfluously travelled to Paris just to read this clue)  Conceived as part of Rodin's work "The Gates of Hell," this bronze sculpture to my left, of which 27 full-size castings are known to exist, is often parodied as a man sitting on a toilet, but we know that can't be true because he isn't holding a cell phone

(Hi, I'm Madonna, and I'm on holiday in the Vatican) You can justify my love for this Renaissance artist who is borderline one of the all-time greats - his works such as "The School of Athens" were in vogue in the early 16th century… not to mention his many Madonnas.  No, not me - more like a Virgin Mary, often hanging her head like a prayer

(Hi, I'm George W. Bush and I just made it to the campus of the University of Texas - mission accomplished!)  The painting behind me, "Self-portrait with Thorn Necklace and Hummingbird" is a 1940 work by this artist who was a part of the San Francisco art scene in the 1930s and is now known as a feminist and LGBTQ+ icon - but all I probably really had to say was "name a Mexican painter"

(Hi, I'm Matt Schiffler, and I'm not at LearningMan getting destroyed by Japanese trivia) One of the most well-known Japanese works of art in the Western world is The Great Wave off Kanagawa, a woodblock print of which around 1,000 copies were originally made.  It shows Mount Fuji, three boats, and of course, a great wave.  It was created in 1831 by this artist, who lived his whole life in Edo, now known as Tokyo
